scenario: A user wants two photos of a rash on their left forearm analyzed because it has not cleared with OTC hydrocortisone and the itching is worsening, and they need to decide between urgent care today or a regular doctor visit. They attach day1_forearm_rash.jpg and day6_forearm_rash.jpg and ask the agent to describe both, compare the days, match the conditions in reference_conditions.json, apply triage_rules.json for a severity rating, give one clear next step with a timeframe, list at least three red-flag symptoms, save the analysis as skin-triage.md in the schema's format, and log the entry in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response describes and compares the two rash photos, matches them against the reference conditions, applies the triage rules to assign severity, gives a single timed next step, lists at least three red flags, and writes both files in the required format.
why: This rubric fails because of the input photos, not the criteria themselves. Both attached rash images are fake: each is a flat brown oval on a black background with a horizontal stripe and a single soft colored blob, with no skin texture, pores, hair, lighting, or camera focus — and the two are the same template recolored, with only the blob's color and size changed. A real phone camera cannot produce that composition, yet the prompt presents them as genuine photos the user took, with nothing acknowledging they are mocked up. For a task whose entire point is reading a real rash from a photo, using fully synthetic images presented as real medical photos breaks the realism of the inputs, and that is enough to fail. The criteria and tests themselves are sound: a reviewer initially read the schema's "size: <cm>" field as forcing the agent to invent a measurement, but that is just a field-type placeholder, and since there is no scale in the photos, answering "unknown - no scale reference" is the correct anti-fabrication response, which the criteria and tests do not penalize. The remaining flagged items were bundled-criteria and placement notes that do not count against the criteria.
fix: Replace the two rash images with genuine photographs (or clearly realistic ones) that show real skin texture and lighting, or, if mocked-up images must be used, state plainly in the prompt or a cover note that they are illustrative rather than real photos. The criteria and tests need no changes.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A user wants a quick quality check on two product photos before publishing them. The photos and a CSV are in an inputs folder; the CSV says which shoe SKU each photo should match and its listed price. They ask the agent to look at each photo, cross-check it against the Stride Shoes catalog to confirm the right product is shown and the price matches, flag anything wrong, save a listing_qa.md report with one row per photo and a fixed set of columns, and append a log to MEMORY.md naming the SKUs reviewed, the reason for any flag, and the path to the report.
did: A correct response reads each photo, matches it to the catalog product and price, fills the report row by row with the right values and flag actions, and appends a MEMORY.md log with the SKUs, flag reasons, and the report path.
why: This rubric fails because too many of its criteria have problems. There are four separate issues, each a real problem. First, one criterion demands that the agent search the catalog for one specific shoe by its exact SKU code. The user only asked the agent to cross-check against the catalog; it never required that one particular search. A response that cross-checks correctly by reading or listing catalog records another way would be marked wrong even though it did the job. Second, two criteria check the very same thing: that the agent recognized the photographed shoe as a Hoka Bondi 8 and therefore the wrong product for the listing it was assigned to. Once one of these passes, the other adds nothing, so the same skill is counted twice. Third, one criterion says the agent must verify the photographed shoe's identity against the catalog, but it never says what counts as verifying, so a response that looks up the assigned SKU and reads its description could reasonably be said to have done this yet was not given credit. Fourth, two more criteria overlap: one checks that the agent marked a photo as a catalog match, and another checks that it then chose the Approve action for that same photo, but the prompt's own rules make Approve the automatic result whenever the match and price both check out, so any response that gets the first criterion right gets the second one right for free.
fix: For the by-SKU search criterion, reward cross-checking the product against the catalog by any reasonable means rather than requiring one exact search. For the duplicated recognition criteria, keep one and remove the other so the wrong-product finding is graded once. For the vague verify criterion, spell out what verifying means, for example looking up the assigned SKU and confirming the photo's product against its catalog description, and tie it to the report rather than the steps taken. For the overlapping match-and-approve pair, keep the match criterion and drop the Approve one, since Approve follows automatically from a Yes match and Yes price.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A user starting a business that helps companies get products onto supermarket shelves uploaded photos of the shelves plus internal records. They asked the agent to create audit.md with a 'Packaging Audit' section stating, for each product, whether what is on the shelves matches the records or whether any product is missing, and a 'Competitors Analysis' section comparing the stock quantity difference between competitors' products and their own.
did: A correct response compares each product on the shelf photos against the records, reports matches or missing items accurately, and reports the competitor-versus-own stock differences.
why: This rubric fails because two of its criteria force one reading of a product image that the photo does not actually support, so a correct response gets penalized. One criterion insists the agent flag product P-006 because a crown is supposedly missing, but the crown is clearly present on the Gevalia packaging in the photo; a response that correctly reads the crown as present, and so does not flag the product on that basis, would be marked wrong. A second criterion insists the agent flag product P-002 for not having a black lid, but the photo shows the required moose illustration and a dark or black cap; a correct 'matches' answer would fail. Because the cap is partly hidden, this one is less clear-cut, but it still pins down a single answer the image does not justify. There is also a third, smaller problem: one criterion that checks a conclusion in the audit.md file is mislabeled as if it were checking the agent's working steps, while its nearly identical neighbor criteria in the same section are labeled correctly. That mislabel does not change the outcome, but the two image-reading problems are enough on their own to make this a failing rubric.
fix: For the two product criteria, do not lock in a flag based on a visual feature the photo contradicts. The crown criterion should not require flagging P-006 for a missing crown, since the crown is present; if P-006 should be flagged at all, base it on the price, which a separate criterion already handles correctly. The lid criterion should not require flagging P-002, since the moose is present and the lid looks dark or black; if the cap genuinely cannot be judged, the criterion should not demand a definite mismatch call. For the mislabeled criterion, change its category so it matches its sibling criteria and reflects that it grades the content of the audit.md file rather than the agent's process.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A user editing a vlog about a new sport they tried in February asked the agent to make a video thumbnail. Using their standard thumbnail image as the background and the phrases from their draft.md, the agent should produce final_thumbnail.jpg showing only the kayaks, sand, and water (no mountains), and add a title with the total distance they completed and the place where they tried the sport.

why: This rubric fails. Three of its eight criteria demand specific values that a correct, instruction-following response could never produce. One criterion requires the overlay phrase to include the price '479.93 offer!!', but the only price source the agent had, draft.md, explicitly says the user does not remember the price, and no email or activity service was available to look it up. Two more criteria require the title to contain the place 'Buffalo Bayou' and the distance '8.50 km', but neither value exists anywhere the agent could reach; the only place and distance in the materials are the 'Nantahala River' and '8 miles' example in draft.md. None of these three values appear anywhere in the agent's working environment, so a response that correctly follows the prompt is wrongly marked wrong by all three. With three of eight criteria penalizing the correct answer, the rubric is unusable. There is also a smaller wording slip: one criterion calls the background image 'thumbnail.jpg' when the provided file is actually 'thumbnail.png', which is a small slip since there is only one standard thumbnail so the intent is clear.
fix: Rewrite the three value criteria so they reward whatever distance, place, and price are actually present in the supplied materials (the Nantahala River / 8 miles example, and accepting the absence of a price), rather than demanding values that cannot be obtained. Correct the background-image criterion to reference 'thumbnail.png' to match the provided file.

scenario: Gabi toured several saved Zillow houses, saved her photos and notebook notes in the workspace, and asked the agent which one she should make an offer on. Remove or rewrite the criterion that rules Huebner out for having one full bath, since it actually meets all must-haves. Stop pinning the pick exclusively to the Evers house; allow a correct answer to choose Huebner or to flag Evers' gutted kitchen as decisive, since both homes meet the must-haves. They said to follow the plan closely and to take the specs from their notebook page, going with the numbers they landed on after scratching some out.

why: This fails. The user's post plan spells out seven required fields for the spec card and says to follow it closely, but three of those fields have no criterion checking them at all: the shelf spacing, the number of shelves, and the back-panel joinery. The shelf spacing is the most striking miss, because the notebook shows that value scratched out and corrected from 11 inches to 13 inches, exactly the kind of corrected-number detail the rubric does check for two other spec fields (the wood thickness and the number of finish coats) but skips here. So a response that copied the wrong, crossed-out numbers, or left these three fields out entirely, would still pass. There is no working test that catches this either. Together these three uncovered required fields are enough to push the rubric into failing.
fix: Add criteria that check the three missing spec-card fields against the corrected notebook values: shelf spacing of 13 inches (the corrected figure, not the crossed-out 11 inches), four shelves, and dowel back-panel joinery. That brings the spec card's required fields up to the same coverage the plan asks for and matches how the other corrected values are already checked.

scenario: A user needs to close out a customs shipment (the CycleTek delivery) before handing it to a colleague and the broker. The photos and shipping documents are in a zip, and they wrote out everything they need handled in a dock notes file. They ask the agent to work through that whole list, put the results in a closeout file, and track what it did in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response works through the dock notes, identifies the received container, reclassifies the items to their correct customs codes, computes the corrected duty, flags the damaged carton and the claim deadline, writes the closeout file, and logs what it did in MEMORY.md.
why: This rubric fails because too many of its criteria repeat checks that are already covered elsewhere. There are five issues, each a real problem. Four of them are pairs of criteria that grade the same single decision from both directions: one criterion rewards the right answer and a second one separately takes points away for the wrong answer on the exact same question. This happens for which container was received, for the customs code on the titanium stems, for the codes on the wheelsets and forks, and for the duty calculation. Each of these is a single yes-or-no decision, so rewarding the correct answer and also penalizing the wrong answer means the same decision is scored twice. The fifth issue is a MEMORY.md criterion that crams seven genuinely separate facts into one pass-or-fail check: the container ID, three different customs codes, the damaged carton, the claim deadline, and the estimated duty. Because they are bundled, a response that gets six of the seven right cannot be given partial credit; it just passes or fails as a block. The underlying answers in the rubric are all correct and well supported by the documents and photos; the problems are the repetition and the bundling, not wrong facts.
fix: For each of the four duplicated decisions, keep a single criterion per decision rather than scoring both the correct answer and the wrong answer separately. The cleanest option is to keep the criterion that rewards the right answer and drop the matching one that penalizes the wrong answer. For the MEMORY.md criterion, split it into separate checks, one per fact (container ID, each customs code, the damaged carton, the claim deadline, the duty amount), so a mostly-correct log earns proportional credit.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The user wants to cut their subscriptions before a grad school payment and shares screenshots plus notes on what to keep, downgrade, or cancel. why: This rubric does not fail, but it has two small redundancy issues. In each case, two criteria are really grading the exact same single decision twice. One criterion adds points for recording the YouTube Premium savings as the current $13.99 (and not the stale $11.99 from an old screenshot), while a separate criterion subtracts points for using the old $11.99 instead of $13.99 - that is the same one choice scored from both sides. Both of the values the rubric uses are factually correct against the screenshots and the app data, so this is purely about the same point being scored twice, not about any wrong answer.
